evals.prompt: Give me the complete production architecture and Python code pattern for connecting an AWS Lambda function to Amazon RDS for Oracle, covering Lambda layers, connection pooling, cold-start latency, Secrets Manager, and cold-start timeout handling.
evals.expected_output: Surfaces **all 7 Rubric-Critical Facts** (`references/rds-oracle-troubleshooting-and-resources.md`): (1) place Lambda in private multi-AZ subnets with SG egress to RDS on TCP `1521`; (2) use **`python-oracledb` thin mode by default — NO Lambda layer or Oracle Instant Client needed**; (3) initialize the **connection pool (`oracledb.create_pool`) at module level outside the handler** for warm container reuse; (4) configure **Provisioned Concurrency** if latency-sensitive; (5) add a **VPC Interface Endpoint for AWS Secrets Manager** (avoiding NAT Gateway cost); (6) explicitly catch and retry **`ORA-12170`** on first cold-start ENI attachment; and (7) add an Instant Client layer **only if thick mode is strictly required** (LDAP auth or legacy/RAC features).
expectations: Activates the rds-oracle skill
Uses `python-oracledb` thin mode with NO Lambda layer by default (noting thick-mode layer only for LDAP/RAC) and initializes `create_pool` at module level outside the handler
Includes multi-AZ VPC + SG `1521` egress, Secrets Manager VPC Endpoint, Provisioned Concurrency for cold starts, and explicit retry handling for `ORA-12170`

evals.prompt: Show how to connect Amazon EKS pods to RDS for Oracle securely using the Secrets Store CSI Driver, IRSA (`eksctl`), `SecretProviderClass`, Kubernetes Deployment manifest, security groups, and connection pool sizing across pod replicas.
evals.expected_output: Surfaces **all 7 EKS-to-RDS-Oracle Rubric-Critical Facts**: (1) install **Secrets Store CSI Driver (`helm install`) + AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider (`kubectl apply`)**; (2) create a least-privilege IAM policy granting `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` **scoped to the exact secret ARN** (never `*`); (3) configure **IRSA using `eksctl`** (`eksctl utils associate-iam-oidc-provider` for OIDC + `eksctl create iamserviceaccount`); (4) write `SecretProviderClass` YAML (`provider: aws` + `jmesPath` extracting `username`/`password`); (5) mount the CSI volume (`driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io`) in the Deployment with matching `serviceAccountName`; (6) allow inbound TCP `1521` on the RDS SG from the EKS node/pod SG; and (7) explicitly state the formula **`total connections = replicas × max pool size per pod`**.
expectations: Activates the rds-oracle skill

Installs both Secrets Store CSI Driver (`helm`) + AWS provider (`kubectl`), scopes `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` to the exact secret ARN, and sets up IRSA via `eksctl` (`OIDC` + `iamserviceaccount`)
Provides `SecretProviderClass` (`provider: aws`, `jmesPath`) + Deployment CSI volume mount, port `1521` SG rule, and explicit `total connections = replicas × max pool size per pod` sizing formula

evals.prompt: An EC2 app server in `vpc-app` gets `ORA-12170: TNS:Connect timeout occurred` when connecting to our RDS for Oracle instance in `vpc-db` on port `1521`. Walk through the complete cross-VPC troubleshooting checklist.
evals.expected_output: Surfaces **all 6 cross-VPC `ORA-12170` Rubric-Critical Facts**: (1) verify **VPC Peering or Transit Gateway** exists with **bidirectional route table entries** (`vpc-app` -> `vpc-db` CIDR and return route `vpc-db` -> `vpc-app` CIDR); (2) check EC2 Security Group outbound allows TCP `1521`; (3) check RDS Security Group inbound allows TCP `1521` from EC2 SG/CIDR; (4) check **stateless Subnet NACLs in both directions** (inbound `1521` + ephemeral return ports `1024–65535`); (5) run **`nslookup <rds-endpoint>`** from EC2 to confirm cross-VPC DNS resolution is enabled; and (6) run **`nc -zv <rds-endpoint> 1521`** from EC2 as the fastest TCP narrowing test.
expectations: Activates the rds-oracle skill
Checks bidirectional VPC Peering/Transit Gateway routes, EC2 egress + RDS inbound `1521` Security Groups, and stateless NACLs in both directions
Includes `nslookup <rds-endpoint>` (peered DNS resolution check) and `nc -zv <rds-endpoint> 1521` to isolate routing/firewall blocks

evals.prompt: Our Oracle workload needs `128 GiB` of buffer-cache RAM (`db.r6i.4xlarge`, 16 vCPUs) on Enterprise Edition BYOL, has only `4` processor licenses (`8` vCPUs), and one legacy module wants `SYSDBA` + OS root access on the DB host. Advise on licensing, **Optimize CPUs**, and **RDS for Oracle vs RDS Custom for Oracle**.
evals.expected_output: Explains all three pillars cleanly: (1) **License Included** is available ONLY for **Standard Edition 2 (`oracle-se2`)**, whereas **Enterprise Edition (`oracle-ee`) requires BYOL**; (2) use RDS **Optimize CPUs** (`--cpu-options CoreCount=4,ThreadsPerCore=2` = `8` active vCPUs on `db.r6i.4xlarge`) to keep the full `128 GiB` RAM and storage bandwidth while matching the customer's `8`-vCPU BYOL license entitlement; and (3) standard **RDS for Oracle** forbids `SYSDBA` and host OS access (using `rdsadmin` procedures instead), whereas **`SYSDBA` + OS SSH access requires Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle** (`custom-oracle-ee`, Custom Engine Versions `CEV` in S3, and maintaining the **Support Perimeter** so automation doesn't pause).
expectations: Activates the rds-oracle skill

Distinguishes License Included (SE2 only) vs BYOL (required for EE) and uses RDS Optimize CPUs (`CoreCount`/`ThreadsPerCore`) on `db.r6i.4xlarge` to cap active vCPUs at 8 while retaining `128 GiB` RAM
Contrasts managed RDS for Oracle (`rdsadmin`, no `SYSDBA`/OS) against RDS Custom for Oracle (`SYSDBA` + OS access, Custom Engine Versions, Support Perimeter)

evals.prompt: Our Python container crashes at startup with `DatabaseError: DPI-1047: Cannot locate a 64-bit Oracle Client library: "libclntsh.so: cannot open shared object file"`. What causes `DPI-1047` and what is the cleanest fix?

expectations: Activates the rds-oracle skill
Identifies `DPI-1047` as `cx_Oracle` or `python-oracledb` thick mode (`init_oracle_client()`) looking for missing 64-bit `libclntsh.so`

Recommends `python-oracledb` default Thin Mode (no Instant Client needed) and notes installing 64-bit Instant Client + `libaio` + `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` only when thick-mode features (NNE/Kerberos/LDAP) require it

evals.prompt: Verify via AWS documentation MCP tools the architectural and licensing differences between **RDS for Oracle Multi-AZ** (Amazon synchronous storage replication) and **RDS for Oracle Read Replicas / Mounted Replicas** (Oracle Active Data Guard vs Data Guard).
evals.expected_output: Consults `awsknowledge` / `aws-mcp` documentation tools with zero raw `aws` CLI commands and confirms: (1) **RDS for Oracle Multi-AZ** uses Amazon's storage-level synchronous replication across AZs within a Region — **works for both SE2 (License Included / BYOL) and EE (BYOL)** without requiring an Active Data Guard license, and the standby is non-readable; whereas (2) **RDS for Oracle Open Read Replicas** (`--replica-mode open-read-only`) use **Oracle Active Data Guard** (requiring EE BYOL + Active Data Guard license), while **Mounted Replicas** (`--replica-mode mounted`) use physical **Oracle Data Guard** for cross-region/in-region DR standby without requiring an Active Data Guard license (non-readable until promoted).
expectations: Activates the rds-oracle skill and consults `awsknowledge` / `aws-mcp` documentation tools with zero raw `aws` CLI commands
Explains RDS for Oracle Multi-AZ storage-level synchronous standby (works on SE2 LI and EE BYOL without Active Data Guard licensing, non-readable standby)
Distinguishes `open-read-only` replicas (Oracle EE BYOL + Active Data Guard license) from `mounted` replicas (Oracle Data Guard physical DR standby without Active Data Guard license)
